title: Trump Appointees Asked a Federal Cybersecurity Agency to Secretly Acquire a Voting Machine — and Hack It
author: Doug Bock Clark
content:
A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees
at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency
focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to
procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be
given to the White House, according to two former administration officials
with knowledge of the request.

The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of
the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the
agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it
uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA
employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any
[election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This
goes against everything CISA represents.”

The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request
was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an
operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government
Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA.

Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried
to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of
its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.

In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more
than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The
president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by
another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.

In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s
ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not
being used to support election security as directed by Congress.

Since Trump signed the CISA Act in 2018, the agency has worked with state
authorities and voting machine vendors to help protect election infrastructure
from cyberattacks. During Trump’s second term, though, CISA has abandoned much
of this work. Several state election authorities said the agency provided them
no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical
planning stages for the upcoming midterms.

“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said
Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as
a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk
of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they
were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.”

While Trump has repeatedly warned that America’s elections are vulnerable to
hacking, in some cases repeating disproven claims, experts said his
administration is undermining the federal government’s role in helping secure
them.

Though CISA re-emerged in September with a last-minute security plan for the
election, some state officials told ProPublica they fear that what is left of
the agency has been compromised by a conspiracy-obsessed presidential
administration. In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020
election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records,
including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state
authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share
information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections.

“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing
relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who
now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way
they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they
ever will in the future.”

A spokesperson for the White House declined an interview request but defended
Trump’s handling of election security in an emailed statement. “President
Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair
elections,” said Lauren Bis.

Bis referred specific questions about CISA’s handling of elections to DHS. DHS
and CISA did not respond to interview requests or to a detailed list of
questions.

> “There’s no fucking way [state governments are] ever going to give any
> information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”
>
> A former federal cybersecurity official who advises state governments

Current and former CISA employees and state election officials describe an
agency that has become significantly less equipped to help states fight
legitimate cyber threats. State leaders say they have used their own resources
to shore up gaps left by CISA, such as paying for sensor technology that can
detect unusual activity in election networks. But some services, like intel on
foreign actors, can’t be replicated. Some people interviewed said they were
worried that Trump and his allies continue to ratchet up rhetoric about voting
security, particularly about threats to voting machines. Officials in one
large voting jurisdiction said they have met privately with machine vendors to
come up with a contingency plan if the federal government seizes their
machines or declares them unusable.

“I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his
administration does,” Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said. “And what
they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.”

* * *

Defending elections from hackers wasn’t always part of DHS’s remit.

Throughout the mid-1990s and 2000s, a series of cyberattacks rocked the
federal government, demonstrating the emerging threat. In 2007, hackers broke
into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. The digital heist, by
an unknown foreign adversary, was so damaging that one intelligence leader
later described it as an [“espionage Pearl
Harbor.”](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/cyber-war-sabotaging-the-
system-06-11-2009/)

Under George W. Bush, DHS underwent a reorganization to more effectively
combat terrorism and respond to disasters like Hurricane Katrina. The
department dedicated resources under an office called the National Protection
and Programs Directorate to help fortify advanced cyber defense systems and
important infrastructure. The office’s work ranged from helping secure events
like the Super Bowl to protecting chemical plants to issuing cybersecurity
warnings to the private sector and the public. In 2018, Trump signed a bill
making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and
transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything
DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.

Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency
did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016
presidential election. Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation
campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media
accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to [bipartisan
reports](https://www.intelligence.senate.gov/2020/08/18/publications-report-
select-committee-intelligence-united-states-senate-russian-active-measures/)
from the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released before the 2020
election. A dozen Russian military agents were indicted for what the Justice
Department described as “a sustained effort to hack into the computer networks
of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Democratic National
Committee, and the presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton.”

Trump publicly downplayed this interference, but DHS leadership saw the Russia
attack as an escalation. In January 2017, before Trump took office, DHS
upgraded America’s elections to the status of critical infrastructure. This
placed the polls and all voting technology used in federal elections under the
watch of what would soon become CISA.

To carry out this function, CISA needed help. But states and voting machine
vendors were wary about sharing data on weaknesses in voting systems, fearing
it could be exploited if certain details were to become public. State
officials were also reluctant to cede any role in election preparation to the
federal government.

Gradually, though, CISA and state election officials negotiated a fragile
trust. At its center was a commitment: The sensitive information states and
vendors shared with CISA would be kept confidential.

“It took years and years of building trust, of talking to election officials,
of hiring people with elections experience who could be validators for the
work that CISA wanted to do, before they finally built strong working
relationships,” said Derek Tisler, who specializes in election security as
counsel for the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, a nonpartisan institute
based out of New York University School of Law.

Under Director Chris Krebs, CISA hosted penetration testing in which its
agents would try to hack into a state’s system to locate weaknesses that could
then be patched, along with tabletop exercises simulating a series of
potential catastrophes around elections. CISA also offered regular secret-
level briefings to secretaries of state to share federal intelligence. And
CISA paid for sensor technology that looked for potential malicious online
activity on election networks, notifying officials about emerging threats.

“The staffing was there, the expertise was there, the visibility was there,
the funding was there,” Macias said.

The consortium shared data as run of the mill as spambots as well as more
serious threats. If Virginia caught unusual activity in its system, it could
let other states know to be vigilant.

While CISA had prepared for attacks from the Chinese and Russian governments,
or lone wolf hackers, few there had expected the threat to elections would
come from inside the White House. But when Trump refused to concede to Joe
Biden in 2020, claiming the vote had been rigged, CISA became a key component
of the guardrails that ultimately led to the election results being certified.

The agency, in a statement co-signed by secretaries of state and voting
machine vendors, vouched for the election’s integrity, calling it “the most
secure in American history.” When Krebs publicly rebutted claims amplified by
the White House as “unsubstantiated” or “technically incoherent,” Trump fired
him over Twitter.

As Congress prepared to vote on certifying the election results, it was
members of CISA, along with the FBI, [who convinced then-Attorney General Bill
Barr](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-midterm-elections-takeover)
that the conspiracy theories embraced by the president could be explained by
human error, not systemic fraud or hacking.

When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, his administration
immediately started to dismantle CISA. The administrative notices were sent
out just a couple of weeks after the inauguration and included the team in
charge of dispelling disinformation.

For the employees under the DOGE microscope, work became impossible, said one
former senior CISA employee. “Those groups couldn’t even order a pizza.”

DOGE laid off people critical to the agency’s election work, including those
who’d worked closely with states. The Trump administration cut funding for the
technology that monitored web and election servers, blinding the federal
government to breaches it had detected.

When it came time for states to prepare for the 2026 midterms, CISA had
disappeared.

* * *

On the evening of July 16, in the Black Hills of South Dakota, dozens of
election officials and their staffs gathered for a reception near Mount
Rushmore. It was the third night of an annual conference for secretaries of
state, drawing participants from red and blue states. They’d spent the week
discussing state voter roll maintenance and voter ID — issues that at times
made for disagreements.

At about 8 p.m., a wave of discomfort swept through the crowd, visible on
attendees’ faces as they glanced frequently at their phones, according to
people at the event. Any minute now, Trump was going to address the nation on
election security. Some at the reception worried he would declare a national
emergency, as his allies had urged him to do months earlier, and use it as a
pretext to direct the government to seize voting machines.

![President Donald Trump stands at a podium in the East Room of the White
House, with the U.S. flag, the presidential flag and a golden curtain behind
him. On either side of him are portraits of Martha and George Washington, in
golden frames. In the foreground are TV and news cameras and a seated
audience.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2285785789_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=2560)President
Donald Trump addresses the nation on national security issues on July 16. Saul
Loeb/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

Then reports on the speech began rolling in, and the mood shifted. The claims
Trump was making were unsubstantiated and outlandish. Many had been examined
ad nauseam, including by those at the reception, and roundly debunked. The
collective anxiety that was palpable moments earlier melted away, as many saw
the speech as another attempt to revive disproved theories unlikely to be
taken seriously by most voters.

“Everyone just sort of guffawed and put their phones away and went to the
bar,” recalled Quinn Raymond, co-founder of VoteShield, a nonprofit that works
with states to help monitor voter registration data, who was at the event.

Still, if the speech made little impact, records published by the Trump
administration to support the president’s claims damaged the already eroding
relationship between CISA and state election officials. The material included
raw information states had shared with the agency that was supposed to remain
private, such as a log of communications from Election Day 2020 detailing
activity being monitored in several states.

“It betrayed the trust of all partners who were willing to share information
at the time,” said Geoff Hale, who worked on CISA’s elections team from the
agency’s inception until last year. Now he specializes in election security at
the Center for Democracy & Technology, a nonprofit that advocates for digital
and civil rights.

Bis, the White House spokesperson, denied that the Trump administration broke
any agreements in releasing the information. “The release of such information
is exactly the sort of transparency news organizations should applaud,” she
said. Bis also defended Trump’s speech, saying it had been fact-checked “by
the agencies whose evidence was released and did not mischaracterize any
information.”

Hale and others said the speech was one of several instances demonstrating the
Trump administration’s reckless attitude toward sensitive data collected by
CISA. Earlier this year, [Politico
reported](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/27/cisa-madhu-gottumukkala-
chatgpt-00749361) that acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala had uploaded
records to ChatGPT, even though DHS had barred its employees from using the
unsecure program. A CISA spokesperson told Politico that Gottumukkala had been
permitted to use the technology for a “short-term and limited” basis.

Last May, [an independent journalist named Brian Krebs
exposed](https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/05/cisa-admin-leaked-aws-govcloud-
keys-on-github/) that CISA published private data, including passwords, cloud
keys and other information, on its public GitHub page, in a folder labeled
“Private-CISA.” A CISA spokesperson told the journalist there was no
indication that sensitive data was compromised.

Some state election authorities were also alarmed to see the lengths to which
the Trump administration went to legitimize the president’s fixation on the
2020 race.

In fall 2025, Missouri election officials produced a memo stating Andrew McCoy
Warner, a Department of Justice official and prominent 2020 election
conspiracy theorist, had called several clerks asking for [access to voting
machines](https://missouriindependent.com/2025/09/02/trumps-doj-wants-access-
to-missouri-voting-equipment-used-in-2020-election/). Tulsi Gabbard, then the
director of national intelligence, had also led an operation in Puerto Rico to
seize election machines. When the private cybersecurity contractor hired to
examine the machines, Mojave Research Inc., failed to find evidence supporting
claims about 2020, [the federal government became
“dissastified”](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/13/politics/voting-
machines-2020-election-odni) with its services and stopped renewing its
contract, its CEO later told reporters.

A spokesperson for the Office of the Director of National Intelligence [told
reporters in August ](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/08/voting-
machine-researchers-say-federal-work-abruptly-ended-after-trump-ally-pushed-
back-their-findings/415300/)that Mojave’s work ceased because it had completed
its contract. Testifying before Congress in March, Gabbard said the seizing of
voting machines came at the request of an assistant U.S. attorney in Puerto
Rico.

“What happened in the second Trump administration is from almost day one — I
mean, literally the first two months — they took all that was built up by
Trump 1 and just decimated it,” said David Becker, founder of the nonpartisan
Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonprofit that works with state
election authorities. “Election officials lost trust in the federal
government.”

It didn’t help that, in his speech, the president mocked CISA’s defense of the
2020 election, calling the statement about it being the most secure in history
a “very pat line” concocted as part of a deep-state cover-up. One former
career CISA employee described being crestfallen at the Trump administration’s
erosion of all they’d accomplished.

“We worked so hard to build that trusted relationship,” said Caitlin
Durkovich, former DHS assistant secretary for infrastructure protection and
co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Civira Partners. “I don’t know how you
put it back together.”

* * *

A few weeks after Trump’s speech, the state election officials gathered once
more, this time for a video call with Nick Andersen, who had replaced
Gottumukkala as CISA’s acting director.

![A man wearing a suit and tie speaks into a
microphone.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2268298926_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=1149)Nick
Andersen, acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security
Agency, at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in
March Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Though the primaries were already under way, this was the first time many had
met Andersen, a former cybersecurity adviser to Trump’s White House who had
joined CISA a year earlier. Andersen is also a district representative for the
Republican Party in Virginia, according to the party’s website. In March, he
gave a speech to the Fairfax GOP chapter titled “Fighting Democrat
Redistricting.”

Speaking over video in August, the boyish-faced former Marine Corps engineer
announced that DHS was preparing to release a plan on how it would work
together with state officials to secure the election, according to five people
who were present at the video meeting, some of whom shared notes with
ProPublica.

Many on the call were stunned at what they perceived as a lack of
understanding of election planning. Early voting for the general election was
just around the corner. They had spent over a year preparing for the midterms,
and there was no more time for ambitious work.

Some peppered Andersen with questions: Where had CISA been when there was
still time to make improvements?

Andersen blamed any lapses or perceived breaches in trust on the federal
government shutdown in fall 2025, twirling his pen uncomfortably and sipping
from a Monster energy drink.

Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, was blunt about his feelings regarding
working with Andersen and CISA, according to several of the people on the
call.

“I told him I didn’t trust him,” Fontes recalled in an interview. “I did raise
my voice a little bit, because I’m frustrated — very frustrated — that they
would have the temerity to come in, clear the entire deck of competent
professionals, stop supporting the states, eviscerate the coordination efforts
that they had and then suddenly come in and say: ‘Oh, we’re from the federal
government. We’re here to help.’”

Indeed, one recently departed CISA official said attempting to do the agency’s
typical election work now would be futile. In previous years, CISA had
finished almost all its preparations with the states by Labor Day.

“That ship has sailed,” the official said.  

CISA [published its security
plan](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/2026-CISA-Election-
Security-Plan-FINAL-508c.pdf) for the 2026 election on Sept. 24. The 13-page
document describes how, over the past two years, CISA has “recommitted to its
statutory mission and remains resolute in strengthening the security of
elections.”

State officials said their planning will ensure a secure election, even
without help from CISA. Yet they and cybersecurity experts worry that Trump
will say the election was hacked if Republicans don’t win in November.

The security plan calls for “leveraging collaborative partnerships” with
states the agency has abandoned since Trump took office. Shenna Bellows,
Maine’s secretary of state, said she’d welcome that but was skeptical of the
agency’s motivations.

“For CISA to promise election officials now, at this point in time, that they
are going to be a resource for the 2026 election is too little, too late,” she
said.

The post [Trump Appointees Asked a Federal Cybersecurity Agency to Secretly
Acquire a Voting Machine — and Hack
It](https://www.propublica.org/article/cisa-election-security-donald-trump)
appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
